episode_appearances.pitch: Custom gift boxes and floral gifts.
episode_appearances.offer: After the other Sharks declined, Mark Cuban offered $150,000 for 20% equity on a non-negotiable basis.

timeline.event: Bouquet Bar launched as a luxury/custom gift-box business in Irvine, according to later company profiles.
Bouquet Bar aired in Shark Tank Season 9, Episode 19; the founders accepted Mark Cuban’s $150,000 for 20% offer.
Dallas Business Journal listed Bouquet Bar inside Mark Cuban’s Shark Tank portfolio and stated Cuban invested $150,000 for 20%.
USPTO TTAB records show Bouquet Bar Inc. obtained extensions of time to oppose Sugarfina trademark applications, confirming continued corporate/IP activity in 2019.
Bouquet Bar Inc., a Delaware corporation, registered as a foreign corporation in California under state ID 04281635, according to California-SOS-derived corporate records.
Later follow-up reporting places the consumer brand’s shutdown in December 2019.
No current operating Bouquet Bar storefront or verified successor operator was located in this bounded research pass.

claims.text: Bouquet Bar is credibly reported to have stopped operating as a consumer gifting brand in December 2019, but the tracker withholds a definitive closure classification because no primary shutdown or current entity record was captured.

The deal-closing record is materially conflicted: contemporary 2018 portfolio reporting and venture data say Cuban invested, whereas newer Shark Tank recap pages say the deal never materialized. Contemporary evidence is weighted more heavily, but executed closing documents remain unavailable.

The existence of a California foreign corporation listed active in a stale 2022-derived record does not contradict a 2019 brand shutdown; legal-entity standing and consumer-brand operation are separate dimensions.

Current public summaries compress or contradict the historical investment narrative. No archived same-page Bouquet Bar capture was retrieved, so no claim is made that a specific page was edited or sanitized.

episode_appearances.pitch: A powered tool for cutting cardboard boxes.
episode_appearances.offer: Kevin O’Leary, with Chip and Joanna Gaines joining, offered $200,000 for 20%. Daniel Lubetzky offered $200,000 for 15% and later withdrew. Reporting also describes a later O’Leary royalty/equity counter; Wright did not accept any offer.

timeline.event: The powered box-cutter invention traces to a 2020 priority date; 214 Central Industries later became the patent applicant/assignee.
214 Central Industries, Inc. filed the BOXBLAYDE federal trademark application; the mark later registered as No. 7462663 on July 30, 2024.
BoxBlayde commercially launched after its Kickstarter campaign; the founder later reported roughly $500,000 of 2024 sales.
A California registry archive source lists 214 CENTRAL INDUSTRIES INC. as registered with company number 6325611.
BoxBlayde appeared in Shark Tank Season 17, Episode 11. Wright asked $200,000 for 5% and ultimately rejected the Sharks’ offers.
BoxBlayde published a first-person post stating it had received multiple Shark offers but deliberately walked away without a deal.
BoxBlayde’s current site, legal policies and marketplace seller records show ongoing sales under 214 Central Industries, Inc.

registry_records.status: current standing unresolved; current legal policies and federal IP records identify the operator
events: California registry archive lists company number 6325611
registry_records.limitation: Direct California BizFile entity detail was not captured. Current company policies and marketplace records consistently identify 214 Central Industries, Inc. as operator.

claims.text: BoxBlayde is operating as of 2026-09-09; founder Rob Wright rejected the Sharks’ offers, so there was no Shark deal to close.
The company’s own dated February 2026 account is direct evidence that no Shark deal was accepted; this is stronger than later generic summaries that merely label the pitch 'no deal.'

The first U.S. powered-box-cutter patent application is currently shown as abandoned, while the BOXBLAYDE trademark registered in 2024. Patent abandonment does not imply the business or product ceased operating.

Current company materials emphasize B2B/retail scale and a commercial product rather than the Kickstarter-stage narrative. No historical same-page archive was obtained, so no claim is made that the company edited or sanitized prior copy.

episode_appearances.pitch: A smart padlock designed to secure home parcel deliveries.
episode_appearances.offer: Lori Greiner proposed a $1,000,000 loan at 8% interest plus 2.5% equity, with a sales royalty until she received $1.5 million back. Brad Ruffkess countered with a larger loan/royalty structure. Lori tried to involve guest Shark Jamie Siminoff; he declined, and Lori withdrew.

timeline.event: BoxLock appeared in the Season 10 premiere. Ruffkess asked $1 million for 5%; Lori ultimately withdrew her financing/equity proposal and BoxLock left without a deal.
BoxLock, Inc. was incorporated/started as a corporation according to BBB; Georgia’s official business-index output assigns control number 20047354 to BOXLOCK, INC.
Federal trademark records identify BoxLock, Inc. as a Delaware corporation with an Atlanta address.
Later financing databases report a Series A round, evidence that BoxLock continued beyond its consumer-Shark-Tank phase.
CB Insights records another venture funding event involving Ideaship.
BoxLock issued current subscription-license terms naming BoxLock Inc. as licensor of its technology.
BoxLock’s current site markets smart padlocks, digital lockout/tagout and industrial access-control software rather than the original porch-delivery consumer use case.

claims.text: BoxLock is operating and has pivoted from consumer parcel security to industrial access control; it received no Shark Tank investment.

BoxLock’s business model materially changed from the 2018 porch-package security proposition to a B2B industrial access-control and digital lockout/tagout platform. This is a verified strategic pivot, not a rename or acquisition.
No Shark investment occurred; Lori Greiner’s proposal was withdrawn on air after Jamie Siminoff declined to join.

Current pages do not preserve the old porch-delivery pitch as the main positioning. Without a captured archived version of those same pages, this demonstrates business-model evolution but not a provable edit to any particular page.

episode_appearances.pitch: A helmet-mounted brake light for motorcycle riders.
episode_appearances.offer: Robert Herjavec made an offer and the founders asked whether Mark Cuban would join; Cuban and Herjavec ultimately offered $200,000 for 20% jointly.

timeline.event: Brake Free began prototype development, according to the company’s current history.
Federal trademark records give March 27, 2017 as first use/first use in commerce for BRAKE FREE.
Brake Free launched its Indiegogo campaign; the company says 2,138 backers supported it.
Brake Free Technologies aired in Season 12, Episode 8; Li and Arkhangelskiy accepted Cuban and Herjavec’s $200,000 for 20% joint offer.
The BRAKE FREE federal trademark registered to Brake Free Technologies, Inc. as registration 6352135.
The company published a dated post framing its path as 'From Shark Tank to Reality' and describing continued operation after the show.
Brake Free published a current founder interview promotion describing its history from the 2017 campaign through Season 12, Episode 8 and dealer expansion.
Current privacy/cookie terms identify Brake Free Technologies, Inc. at a Broomfield, Colorado address.
Brake Free’s official site remains active with products and dealer-partnership recruitment.

claims.text: Brake Free Technologies is operating; the accepted $200,000 Mark Cuban/Robert Herjavec investment for 20% is strongly corroborated as completed, though executed closing documents were not found.

The accepted on-air Cuban/Herjavec deal is verified by ABC video/episode evidence; post-show closing is strongly corroborated by later reporting that calls the Sharks investors, but executed deal documents were not found.

The business remains active independently of the Shark deal question: current terms identify the corporation, the federal trademark remains registered, and the company is actively selling/recruiting dealers.
